title: Iron mind weightlifting straps review
summary: NH reviews IronMind lifting straps after almost two years of use: how to assemble them correctly so the strap runs between thumb and index, their durability, grippy texture, how they harden with age, and their ideal length. He argues non-competing bodybuilders should use straps and recommends sticking with one good pair.

claims.claim: Straps take grip out of the equation so you only focus on your back and leg drive.
If you're a bodybuilder who doesn't compete in powerlifting, use straps; there's no reason not to.
Straps must be assembled correctly so that when wrapped, the hand holds the bar with the strap underneath; done wrong they feel strange and tug on the wrist.
Correctly worn, the strap passes between the index finger and thumb; if it runs outside the wrist when tightened, it's on the wrong hand.
NH has used IronMind straps for almost two years without any sign of breaking, whereas he has seen other straps snap mid-pull.
A strap's texture matters: silky straps feel like they'll slip and mentally check you out; IronMind's grainy texture feels like knurling.
Pricier durable straps beat $5 straps; changing straps often throws training off, so stick with one pair.
Straps stiffen and take a permanent bend with sweat over months (he never washes his); he finds them too soft new and better once broken in like shoes.
Months of barbell friction wore away only about 1/20-2/20 of the strap; he expects several more years of use.
The ideal strap length lets you loop it two or three times around the bar; much longer straps are pointless and shorter ones less secure.
Gripping the bar all the time leads to fewer gains, especially for the upper back.
